title: 6 days Upper Body dominant split review (MMA focus)
summary: NH reviews a viewer MMA fighter's six-day home program built around 130 lb of weights and bands. He praises the minimalist, upper-body-dominant structure for an athlete who must save energy for sparring, while tweaking rep ranges toward evolving schemes (3-5 sets of 8-12), criticizing floor presses and standing barbell extensions, and explaining why lower body work should stay limited for fighters.
claims: With only 130 lb of free weights, rep ranges must stay higher because intensity cannot be raised by stacking weight
A bench and a squat rack are non-negotiable for full chest and leg development
Weight training is never as specific as sport practice, but it builds injury resilience, athleticism and strength that you then use in the sport
Lifting six days a week on top of MMA taxes recovery; lower the frequency if needed
He dislikes training blocks for bodybuilders, but martial artists can periodize: more lifting early, tapering toward competition as sparring increases
A shoulders-and-back day looks unsynergistic but works because the overhead press warms the upper back before pull-ups, face pulls and raises
Overhead press template: 6 sets, 3 intensity sets of 2-3 reps plus 3 volume sets of 5 reps about 20-25 lb lighter
You can never do too many pull-ups if you protect your tendons; they are very safe, decompress the spine and pair well with overhead press, which loads the lumbar spine
5x5 is acceptable but he prefers 3x5, and evolving rep ranges even more
Banded face pulls 4x25 are ideal; high reps let you sense mechanical failure, and face pulls done with postural failure reinforce bad posture
Lateral raises at 4x20 are a good range to control the weight instead of swinging it
The upper back should be trained almost every day at varying intensities (not heavy shrugs or rack pulls daily); without lower back involvement it tolerates huge volume
With limited weight, back squats should go to 4x8-12 rather than 4x8
Banded squats can be taxing on the shoulders; Dave Tate hurt his shoulders that way
Dumbbell lunges suit fighters by mimicking fight positions, and are safer heavy than barbell lunges because you can drop the dumbbells
Jump squats after heavy lower work train you to stay explosive while tired, which fighting demands
Dumbbell floor press is a subpar dumbbell bench lacking the bottom stretch; he did it for three years and got poor chest results
Standing barbell triceps extensions stress the wrists and give little stretch
Supersetting biceps and triceps is a must for arm growth; which comes first changes performance and results, so experiment
Shoulder endurance keeps a fighter's guard up late in rounds, and punching power comes partly from the upper back
When running evolving schemes, evolve the reps before the sets
Static rep ranges become more useless the higher the reps; if you get 8 reps on set one and set three of 3x8, you sandbagged
Pair 3-5 sets with an 8-12 rep range rather than 8-10 so the set and rep evolution have room to manipulate volume
He never counts pull-ups and takes every non-warm-up set to failure
Shoulders can take a massive amount of volume because of their three heads, even though their high mobility makes them injury-prone
A 5x8 deadlift is a bad rep range unless you lack enough weight to make lower reps challenging
A dumbbell deadlift is close to a deficit trap bar deadlift; he did them for years for lack of choice
A rigid core is always valuable, even if some floor-pull muscles are less useful for fighting
Two AMRAP sets of push-ups and rows after dips are enough when pre-fatigued; the fibers are trashed and it is time to go home
For fighters an upper-body-dominant split (4 upper, 2 lower days) makes sense because lower body lifts tax the CNS, tendons and recovery more
exercises: 3 heavy sets of 2-3 + 3 volume sets of 5
subpar: no bottom stretch, poor chest results
similar to deficit trap bar deadlift
